summary.text: Vieta's formulas relate the coefficients of a polynomial to sums and products of its roots.
They provide relations between the roots without having to compute the roots themselves.
They are named after the 16th-century French mathematician François Viète, who derived them for the case of positive roots.

paragraphs.heading: What the formulas say
paragraphs.text: Vieta's formulas connect a polynomial's coefficients with what you get by adding and multiplying its roots. They are useful because they tell you how the roots relate to each other without your having to work out the roots first. So you can learn about the roots of an equation you have not solved.

paragraphs.heading: The quadratic case
paragraphs.text: Take a quadratic, P(x) = ax² + bx + c, with roots r₁ and r₂. Vieta's formulas say that r₁ + r₂ = −b/a and r₁r₂ = c/a. The first rule also helps locate the lowest or highest point of P.

paragraphs.heading: Where they come from
paragraphs.text: Any polynomial a₀xⁿ + a₁xⁿ⁻¹ + ⋯ + aₙ of degree n can be split into factors as a₀(x − r₁)⋯(x − rₙ), where the r's are its roots. If you multiply those factors back out and match up equal powers of x, each coefficient turns out to be built from the roots. For a quadratic written a₂x² + a₁x + a₀, the matching gives r₁ + r₂ = −a₁/a₂ and r₁r₂ = a₀/a₂.

paragraphs.heading: The general pattern
paragraphs.text: For a polynomial of any degree, the rule is aᵢ = (−1)ⁱ a₀ Eᵢ⁽ⁿ⁾(r₁, …, rₙ). Here Eᵢ⁽ⁿ⁾ is the ith elementary symmetric polynomial: add up every product you can make from i of the roots, each using different roots. So the second coefficient involves the sum of the roots, the next involves the sum of products of pairs, and so on, with the sign switching each step.

paragraphs.heading: A warning case
paragraphs.text: Some care is needed when the number system, or ring, you work in is not an integral domain. In the integers modulo 8, the polynomial x² − 1 has four different roots, namely 1, 3, 5 and 7. It factors both as (x − 1)(x − 7) and as (x − 3)(x − 5). Because it does not equal (x − 1)(x − 3), the formulas cannot be used with the roots 1 and 3 together.

paragraphs.heading: Who found them
paragraphs.text: The formulas carry the name of François Viète, a 16th-century French mathematician also known by the Latin form Franciscus Vieta. He worked them out for the case where the roots are positive. His methods were very close to those of the 12th-century mathematician Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi. Girard has been described as the first to grasp in general how the coefficients come from sums of the roots and their products.
